The best chain on garnet is QB7-QB12-QB11, with QB12 in the middle. I read the current default garnet calibration (set f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade). It lists IRB CZ fidelities for all 28 CZ pairs. I then scored every chain of 3 connected qubits. The QB7-QB12 pair has fidelity 0.99802. The QB12-QB11 pair has fidelity 0.99869. Their product is 0.99671, which is the highest of all chains. The next best chain is QB12-QB11-QB16, with a product of 0.99469.

I built a 3-qubit GHZ circuit in IQM's native gates on exactly those qubits. All three qubits get a PRX(pi/2, pi/2) rotation. A CZ on QB12-QB7 is followed by PRX(-pi/2, pi/2) on QB7. A CZ on QB12-QB11 is followed by PRX(-pi/2, pi/2) on QB11. The circuit uses no other two-qubit gates, and it measures all 3 qubits. I simulated it locally first. A perfect quantum computer would give 000 half the time and 111 half the time.

I ran it on garnet:mock with 200 shots as job 01a16042-d6d9-7674-9b97-9bbe33e215e8. The job completed. The counts are 000: 37, 001: 69, 110: 48, and 111: 46, with bits in the order QB7, QB12, QB11. These counts do not look like a GHZ state. The reason is that the mock returns random results that do not depend on the circuit. The mock only checks that the server accepts the job. A mock job costs 0 credits.

The principle is that a GHZ state links three qubits so that they agree on every shot: all 0 or all 1. Each CZ gate adds some error. Picking the chain whose CZ fidelities have the highest product gives that agreement the best chance of surviving on real hardware. Running the same circuit on real garnet would show whether it does. That run would cost credits, so I did not do it.
